brief.head: Friends in tiers
brief.text: Ajay Shah, citing Dunbar’s number, makes deliberate effort for his closest few. Friendships have their moments, he said: “no man walks in the same friendship twice.” {017-C01}

brief.head: Dream, don’t count
brief.text: Technology and GDP will probably improve, Ajay Shah said, but a society’s progress is far more complex. Many countries have gone terribly wrong, so it is not guaranteed. {017-C03}

brief.head: Unlikely is inevitable
brief.text: Lose five poker hands in a row as an 80 per cent favourite and you may cry foul. Given enough hands, Amit Varma said, such runs are bound to happen. {017-R12}

brief.head: Patriots at the board
brief.text: Amit Varma’s patriots are the top Russian chess players who wrote against Putin after the invasion. Many can no longer enter Russia and now play for other countries. {017-S07}

brief.head: Beyond any gamer
brief.text: For an AI researcher in China the export controls are a catastrophe, Ajay Shah said. But the chips barred are “way beyond anything a gamer will want”. {#gamer}

thought.text: Standing by your country is not standing by the state.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, disagreeing after the fact with a scholar who quit to stand by his country

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah on globalisation’s rise, fall and return
lead.head: Still global, now with a bouncer
body: Many people have written globalisation’s obituary. Ajay Shah, who coined a term for what is happening instead, thinks they are wrong. “It’s not true that globalization is dead,” he said, “but that the perimeter has shrunk.” {017-C11}

Talking to Amit Varma, Shah told the story in waves: a first globalisation of near-total freedom, a long dark chapter ruled by nation states, a second that welcomed everyone, and now a third that asks its members to behave.
## Five flows, two forces
Shah began by taking the tired word apart. Globalisation, he said, is about five things crossing borders through voluntary transactions: ideas, people, goods, services and capital. {017-C04}

Two forces push it up and down. One is the state, which bans books, issues passports, levies customs duties and imposes capital controls. The other is technology. “It’s about the death of distance,” Shah said.
Varma put the philosophical question plainly. If friends in Mozambique and Pune both want to sell you ball bearings in Mumbai, he asked, why should it be harder for the one in Mozambique?
## Paradise lost, and regained

Steamships, the Suez Canal and the telegraph set off the first globalisation. States stayed out of the way. People travelled without passports, and capital raised in London flowed downhill to the United States, Argentina and India, where returns were higher.

Nationalism destroyed it. The First World War brought passports and blockades, Hitler imposed the world’s first capital controls, and the post-war order designed by John Maynard Keynes and Harry Dexter White traded free capital for fixed exchange rates.
The world’s trade-to-GDP ratio, Shah said, only got back to its 1913 level in 1982. “We lost freedom from 1913 to 1982, or maybe even a bit beyond.” {017-C06}
The second globalisation that followed brought container ships, wide-body aircraft, computers and telecom. India’s software and services boom, Shah said, came from plugging into it.
## Rules of the club
Then came economic statecraft: chips that may not be sold to China, Dutch machines that may not be shipped there, Russian central bank reserves grabbed after the invasion of Ukraine.

The second globalisation had let everyone in without conditions. “We felt confident that as you become rich, you will inevitably stop beating your wife,” Shah said. Instead China grew more authoritarian, and Gorbachev’s Russia became Putin’s.

Now, he argued, the advanced economies, which include Japan, Taiwan and South Korea, make good behaviour a condition of entry, starting with not invading your neighbour. About 85 per cent of world GDP is inside the club, and there globalisation is deepening. {#club85}
Shah is not fussed. India, he said, is a status quo power that has no wish to conquer Bangladesh. His advice, borrowed from Deng Xiaoping: “bide your time.”
Varma was less comfortable. Those shut out, he said, are not rogue nations but “unfortunate people who happen to be in countries which have rogue regimes.”
On one thing the two agreed. Trade deficits, as Tim Harford’s babysitter shows, are no problem at all: individuals and firms trade, not countries. {017-C13}
The episode began with friendship and Dunbar’s number. It ended with Varma weeping in the rain over a podcast, and Shah lost in a book in an Irani cafe until 9 pm.

second.label: Randomness
second.head: Too random to be random
second.deck: Apple fixed its shuffle by breaking it, Amit Varma told Ajay Shah
body: When the iPod was first introduced, its shuffle played songs truly at random. Some listeners complained: they had got six Bruce Springsteen songs in a row, and that could not be random.

“Given a long enough number of iterations,” Amit Varma said, “any unlikely thing will happen.” {017-C16} Apple’s answer was an algorithm that broke up such streaks, so the shuffle would appear random without being random. {017-S03}

Ajay Shah offered the statistician’s view. The runs test checks randomness by counting how often streaks of different lengths occur. {#runstest} Fed data from the original iPod, he said, it would have delivered an objective verdict: “Apple, you are lying.”

quote.text: So how Apple dealt with this complaint was by introducing an algorithm which made it non-random

second.caption: the too-random iPod

third.head: Soaked in a war story
body: Amit Varma started Dan Carlin’s World War One series, *Blueprint for Armageddon*, on a run. {017-R23} When his one-hour workout ended he could not go back up to his apartment, and stood below, still listening.

On another run it began to rain, and he stayed out. That day Carlin read the letters a group of soldiers wrote to their wives and girlfriends the night before a battle in which they all died. {017-S05}
“And I was weeping in the rain,” Varma said. The series has no script and no sound effects: just one man talking, “practically thinking aloud”.
It taught him that a story needs nothing but a voice. Storytelling was humanity’s first entertainment, he said. “Audio is the most powerful medium in the world.” {017-C18}
third.caption: Dan Carlin’s war letters

p2.title: Three globalisations
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s history of a world that opened, closed and reopened with conditions, argued over with Amit Varma

sections.label: The moral circle
sections.head: Who counts as one of us
sections.caption: the expanding circle
body: Before ships and telegraphs could join the world, Amit Varma argued, there was a globalisation of the mind. He took the idea from W.E.H. Lecky’s *History of European Morals*: the expanding circle. {017-R02}

Humans, Lecky said, begin by extending moral consideration to a small circle, the family. Over history it widens to friends, the tribe, the nation and beyond. Everyone outside it, Varma said, “might as well be animals”.
That explains horrors such as slavery, he said: the circle had not yet grown beyond people’s own kind or skin colour. At one point it may not even have included women.
## Next, the animals

Peter Singer argues that the circle should reach animals. Varma expects it will: just as Jefferson kept slaves and thought it morally fine, people two hundred years from now may look back on us and say “oh they ate animals.” {017-J13}
But circles can also contract. With so much nationalism and so much virulence about identity, he said, “our circles are shrinking and not expanding, and that worries me greatly.” {017-C02}

~ Ajay Shah, for his part, marvelled that Mahavir and Jainism emerged in a primitive society short of protein, which was no golden age. There, he said, some people “developed very advanced concepts and philosophies”.

quote.text: So it’s a very iffy thing, it’s something to aspire for. We should dream of it, but we should not count on it.

sections.label: Defining terms
sections.head: Five things that cross borders
sections.caption: what globalisation means
body: “By the time a word graduates into the airport books,” Ajay Shah said, “it surely stops making much sense.” {017-J09} So he took globalisation apart.
Globalisation, he said, is the extent to which five flows, arising from voluntary transactions, are not shaped by a national border: ideas, people, goods, services and capital.

States interfere with each. They ban books and ideas to push a convenient narrative. They give every individual a number and put up a check post at the border, a game Shah said began at the time of the First World War. They charge customs duties on ball bearings from Mozambique.
## The small chicken

And they control capital intricately. In India, Shah said, poultry farms and nanotechnology firms may borrow abroad but others cannot. Amit Varma spotted the opportunity: “If you’re a really small chicken, you have the best of both worlds, poultry farms and nano chicken.” {017-J01}
Against the state stands technology. Container ships and air freight made it possible to move ball bearings from Mozambique to India, and telecom made services exportable.
~ The state itself, Shah reminded listeners, is simply “the community that achieves and maintains a monopoly of physical violence in a given territory”. {#state}

quote.text: the term globalization refers to the extent to which these five things are not being shaped by a national border.

sections.label: Wave one
sections.head: Capital rolls downhill
sections.caption: the first globalisation
body: Steamships, the Suez Canal and the telegraph set off the first globalisation, Ajay Shah said, as messages, money and cotton began moving between the United States, the UK and India. {017-C05}
People travelled without passports or visas, and a lawyer could go and practise in London. The only constraints were those of technology.

An important feature, Shah said, was capital moving downhill. London had so much capital that one more factory there earned little, while returns in the United States, Argentina and India were high. Projects everywhere raised money in London and invested it where it earned more.
## The long dark chapter

“All this went to hell,” Shah said, with the First World War and the Russian Revolution. Passports arrived, Britain blockaded Germany, and German submarines fired on cargo ships. Hitler, wanting to go after the Jews, brought in the world’s first capital controls. {017-J12}

After 1945, John Maynard Keynes and Harry Dexter White designed GATT, the World Bank and the IMF around fixed exchange rates. Keynes knew intuitively, Shah said, that you cannot manage the exchange rate and have an open capital account. {#keynes} So capital controls stayed.
~ Amit Varma added that Keynes once wanted Chintaman Deshmukh as the IMF’s first managing director, until the Americans objected: “What Indian fellow, what are you talking about?” {017-J11}

quote.text: It’s important to remember that in the first globalization, nation states were not in the game.

sections.label: Wave two
sections.head: When the state stepped aside
sections.caption: the second globalisation
body: From 1982, Ajay Shah said, the freedoms lost since the First World War began to return. Container ships and wide-body aircraft cut transport costs, computers and telecom made services tradable, fixed exchange rates gave way to floating ones, and capital controls came off.
Within the European Union, visa-free travel let people take a bus across national borders. India, Shah said, was “a gigantic beneficiary”: its software and services revolution came from plugging in.
## Better at both

Why does trade help? David Ricardo showed, Shah said, that it raises welfare even when one side is better at everything. What matters is a difference in the ratio of how much better each side is at two things. {017-C08}
Amit Varma offered his own version: “I am a better podcaster than you. I am also a better economist than you.” Yet he does the podcasting and leaves the economics to Shah. {017-J02}

Shah’s test from public economics: intervention is justified only by a market failure, such as asymmetric information, an externality or a public good. Buying ball bearings from Mozambique involves none of these. Without one, he said, intervention harms welfare and GDP. {017-C09}
~ Varma added that a tariff redistributes from poor consumers at large to rich interest groups, and that voluntary trade is consent, a positive-sum game that state coercion spoils.

quote.text: when the state intervenes in the absence of a market failure it has an adverse impact on welfare.

sections.label: Wave three
sections.head: Don’t invade your neighbour
sections.caption: economic statecraft
body: In recent years, Ajay Shah said, things once unimaginable have begun to happen, under a field called economic statecraft: using state power to interfere with the working of the economy. {#statecraft}

The United States blocked Chinese purchases of American businesses and Dubai Ports World’s purchase of a port. It barred top-end chips from sale to China. With European governments, it stopped ASML, a Dutch maker of machines costing about $150 to 200 million each, from selling to Chinese buyers. {#asml}
After Russia invaded Ukraine, about $600 billion of its central bank’s reserves held abroad were grabbed, and many Russian entities were cut off from SWIFT. {#reserves}
## An audience of one

The moral case, Shah said, is that choking an aggressor economically costs fewer lives than fighting with guns. And the response to Russia was meant for an audience of one, Xi Jinping: don’t you dare invade Taiwan. {017-C10}

Plenty of writers have declared globalisation dead. Shah disagrees. Rogue states such as Russia, China, Iran and North Korea face the toolkit. For Japan, Dubai or India, globalisation is great, and after COVID firms realised remote workers could just as well be in India.
~ Nor, he argued, can any coalition of countries build a currency or payment system to rival the dollar and the euro.

quote.text: And the trade-off your moral calculus is between the deaths of soldiers and civilians versus the career destruction for an AI researcher in China.

sections.label: The babysitter
sections.head: In deficit, and delighted
sections.caption: trade deficits and babysitters
body: Amit Varma brought a third angle to the economics and geopolitics: babysitters. In a 2005 *Financial Times* column, Tim Harford noted that he pays his babysitter all the time and she buys nothing from him. {017-R18}
Treat them as countries and you would see a trade deficit, Varma said. In fact they are two individuals transacting to mutual benefit, just like Indians buying from Chinese firms.

Ajay Shah called each deal a double thank-you moment. The Indian importer tells his girlfriend he got a great deal; the Chinese exporter tells her boyfriend the same. “Everyone has a good romantic life in your stories,” Varma observed. {017-J04}
## Count the haircut

Shah asked that goods and services be counted together, since a widget, a potato and a haircut are all things you sell. That balance equals the current account deficit, which means capital is coming in. He would welcome capital inflows of 10 to 20 per cent of GDP a year. {017-C14}
Varma’s disquiet was for those outside the club: the average Russian patriot, not fond of what Putin is doing, who still cannot get his McDonald’s burger. {#mcdonalds}
~ Pleased by Shah’s words, Varma still refused the blessing “aapke muh mein ghee shakkar”. Ghee is a superfood, he said; “avoid shakkar, it is poison.” {017-J05}

quote.text: It is individuals, it is firms that do trade, not countries that do trade.

side.boxTitle: A term of Ajay Shah’s own
side.boxText: Ajay Shah set out the idea in his article *Dawn of the third globalisation?*: a world still globalising, but inside a club with rules. The first and second globalisations are in the literature, Amit Varma noted; the third is a term Shah coined. {#coined}

contQuote.text: And I will borrow a piece of advice from the great man Deng Xiaoping, which is bide your time. For 100 years, our journey is to become an advanced economy and a democracy.

stories.caption: Polson’s rancid butter
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on Polson, Amul and the taste of a bad train ride
stories.head: A butter too fresh for Bombay
body: During the First World War, the British Army wanted vast amounts of butter. Polson, a British company that grew up in India, built the first milk supply chain out of Gujarat, sending butter by train to Bombay and on to the UK. {#polson}
After the war Polson turned to the Indian market, and it dominated butter into the 1960s and early 70s. “As a child, I have eaten Polson butter,” Ajay Shah said.

Then came Amul. Kurien’s cooperative movement in Gujarat, with technical and financial support, Shah believed, from Denmark’s development aid agency, put new machines and process designs into the milk supply chain. Chilling plants and refrigerated vans carried clean, high-quality butter to Bombay.
Bombay hated it. The first batches flopped. Next to Polson, the city found Amul bland and dull: it did not have the punch of butter.

Investigators traced the cause to the railway. Refrigeration on the trains was poor, so Polson’s butter always arrived from Gujarat a little rancid. “And the tastes of the Bombay consumer had become programmed to expect butter to taste a little rancid,” Shah said. {017-S01}

Amul had failed, in short, because it was too good. So scientists worked out the exact chemicals that form when butter goes rancid and added them to Amul’s. Shah did not know whether they persist to this day.
~ Amul took off in Bombay and drove Polson out of business. Amit Varma summed up the method: “They made it rancid deliberately.”
stories.why: A wartime supply chain shaped Bombay’s palate for half a century, and what the city called taste was a side effect of bad refrigeration. A better product can lose until it reproduces the flaws its customers have learned to expect.
stories.postscript: Varma’s counter-story: Apple made its iPod shuffle less random so that it would feel random. {017-S03}

stories.start: circa 1980s, right, there is a department in the Tamil Nadu government called CCA
stories.end: I think I got it from a book by Bibek Debroy
stories.caption: Churchill’s Tamil Nadu cigars
stories.kicker: The story Amit Varma must tell, or his brain explodes
stories.head: A budget for Churchill’s ghost
body: In the 1980s, Amit Varma said, a department of the Tamil Nadu government called the CCA asked for a bigger budget: its allocation had been stagnant for a long time. A curious bureaucrat went looking for its origins.

They lay in the Second World War. Winston Churchill could not get his favourite Cuban cigars, and the world’s second-best cigars, Varma said, came from a town in Tamil Nadu. India was still British, so a department was set up to supply him: the Churchill Cigar Assistant.

Then, in Varma’s words, “World War II ended, Winston Churchill died, India gained independence, not in that order.” {017-J06} The department lived on into the 1980s, and “the person in it has the audacity to say we need more budget.” {017-S02}
~ Varma credits the story to a book by Bibek Debroy.
stories.why: A supply chain born of a wartime shortage survived its only customer for decades. Once a government body exists, it keeps justifying itself long after anyone remembers why it was created.

stories.start: There is an island in the ocean where in nineteen fourteen
stories.end: trying to stop intruders, and obviously it was an isolated island
stories.caption: Hiroo Onoda’s 29-year watch
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Walter Lippmann and a soldier left behind
stories.head: On guard for a finished war
body: Amit Varma read from the first chapter of Walter Lippmann’s *Public Opinion*. In 1914 a few Englishmen, Frenchmen and Germans lived on an island where the British mail steamer came only once in sixty days. {#sixtydays}
The war had broken out, and for six weeks nobody there knew. “For six strange weeks they acted as if they were friends, when in fact they were enemies,” Lippmann wrote. {017-C17}

It reminded Varma of Hiroo Onoda, a Japanese soldier who landed on an island in the Philippines around 1944 with orders to defend it until death. “No one told him the war was over,” Varma said. For twenty-nine years he guarded it. {017-S04}
~ Varma first heard the story in Dan Carlin’s *Supernova in the East*. Lippmann’s chapter is called “The World Outside and the Pictures in Our Heads”.
stories.why: Lippmann’s point, as Varma used it: people act on the pictures in their heads, not on the world outside. Without information, his examples showed, a man can spend decades fighting a war that has already ended.
stories.postscript: Varma said no technological change has made Lippmann’s book, published at least a century ago, obsolete.

stories.start: I was standing in Strandbook Stall in Bombay, and at random
stories.end: book. This is the life to live this is the good life.
stories.caption: a book read in an Irani cafe
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s pick: a book he could not put down
stories.head: Rush hour can wait
body: Ajay Shah was in Strand Book Stall in Bombay, with reason to hurry. He was due back in Bandra, and in rush hour, the sooner you left, the sooner you got home.
At random he came across David Kahn’s *Seizing the Enigma*. He read the first one or two pages, decided “this works”, and bought it. {017-R24}
Outside, those pages had left him transfixed. He wandered aimlessly for a little while, then gave up, found a local Irani shop, sat down and read the whole book until 9 pm.
~ “The only one life I could imagine at that moment was to drop everything and sit in an Irani shop and finish the book,” he said. Amit Varma’s verdict: “This is the good life.” {017-S06}
stories.why: A great book can override every plan for the day. Shah offered the tale as his recommendation, a companion to Varma’s weeping in the rain, and Varma saw it as the good life.

quiz.q: Why did Bombay first reject Amul’s butter, according to Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: It was too good: Bombay was used to Polson’s slightly rancid butter.

quiz.q: What did the Tamil Nadu government department called the CCA originally do?
quiz.a: It supplied Tamil Nadu cigars to Winston Churchill during the Second World War.

quiz.q: Which five things crossing borders define globalisation in Ajay Shah’s account?
quiz.a: Ideas, people, goods, services and capital, moving through voluntary transactions.

quiz.q: In which year, by Shah’s account, did world trade-to-GDP regain its 1913 level?
quiz.a: 1982: freedom was lost, Shah said, from 1913 to 1982 or beyond.

quiz.q: What did Tim Harford’s babysitter show about trade deficits, as Amit Varma told it?
quiz.a: He pays her, she buys nothing from him, and both are better off.

quiz.q: Whose advice did Ajay Shah borrow for India in the third globalisation?
quiz.a: Deng Xiaoping’s: bide your time, and become an advanced economy first.
